title: Amazing grace
hookLine: John Newton, a slave-ship captain, later becomes a pastor and joins the abolitionists

cards: Wretch is a strange word to find in a song people sing at funerals and at weddings. That saved a wretch like me. The man who wrote it didn't mean it as a figure of speech.
He had been a sailor, a slave trader, and the captain of ships that carried captured Africans across the Atlantic in chains. Later he became a pastor in a small English village.
Later still, he stood up in public, said the trade he had worked in was wicked, and wanted it ended.

teach.h: THE STORM WAS NOT THE END.
teach.b: John Newton's story is often told as a sudden turn: a storm at sea, a terrified prayer, a changed man. That storm did matter to him. But the honest version is slower and harder.
After it, Newton kept working in the slave trade, and even captained slave ships, while reading his Bible and keeping a prayer journal. Faith came first. Seeing what he had done came much later.
In time he left the sea, was ordained in the Church of England, and served as curate in the village of Olney, where he and the poet William Cowper wrote hymns for their congregation.
That's where Amazing grace comes from: "Amazing grace! (how sweet the sound) That sav'd a wretch like me! I once was lost, but now am found, Was blind, but now I see." Listen for the Gospels in it.

teach.h: LOST AND FOUND, BLIND AND SEEING.
teach.b: Lost and found is the father's cry over the prodigal son in Luke: "he was lost, and is found." Blind but now I see is the man Jesus healed in John, answering his questioners: "whereas I was blind, now I see."

Then Newton did something harder than writing a hymn. Years after leaving the trade, he published a pamphlet describing what he had seen on the ships, confessing he had taken part, and condemning the trade.
He supported William Wilberforce and the campaign to end it. Grace, in Christian teaching, is God's love freely given, never earned. In Newton's life it didn't erase the past.
It made him able, finally, to look at it.

how: Amazing Grace is sung across Protestant, Catholic and other churches, at Sunday services, funerals and public gatherings, and Newton is remembered in the Church of England's story of the campaign against the slave trade.

games.q: you're John Newton, now a respected pastor. your past in the slave trade is behind you. a campaign to end the trade is growing. what do you do?
o: keep quiet; the past is forgiven.
publish what you saw and confess your part.
games.why: Newton published a pamphlet describing the ships, confessing his part, and supported the campaign to end the trade.

practice: Think of a wrong you once defended: something you argued for, excused or laughed along with, that you see differently now. Name it plainly to yourself, without excuse and without beating yourself up.
If you pray, bring it to God in your own words, or with Newton's line, I once was lost.
